To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in men, increased cortisol production rates and free cortisol levels correlate with visceral fat accumulation and decreased insulin sensitivity.

increased endogenous cortisol production rates, which are associated with visceral fat and impaired insulin sensitivity, are maintained with weight loss and may contribute to increased visceral fat and insulin insensitivity after diet-induced weight reduction.

increased cortisol production rates, cortisol levels, and 11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrongenase type 1 expression in subcutaneous adipose tissue are associated with increased visceral adiposity and insulin resistance and that these relationships are maintained after weight loss.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship of cortisol to body fat distribution, insulin resistance and weight loss in men.
the role that cortisol plays in obesity and insulin resistance, and the relationship between cortisol and 11beta-hsd-1.
the relationship between the hypothalamic-pittuitary-adrenal axis and obesity and insulin resistance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
increased cortisol production is not a cause of visceral fat and insulin insensitivity, but rather a consequence of visceral fat and is a predictor of the ability to lose weight.
the hypothalamic-pittuitary-adrenal axis is a key regulator of body fat distribution and insulin resistance in obesity.
cortisol production and free levels correlate with abdominal fat and insulin resistance, but weight loss does not affect these measures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cortisol production and free cortisol levels are associated with increased visceral fat and decreased insulin sensitivity in men.
the increased cortisol production rates in men with obesity is not a result of obesity, but rather a cause of it.
cortisol production rates are increased in obese men and correlate with visceral fat accumulation, insulin resistance, and 11β-HSD1 expression in subcutaneous adipocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cortisol production rates, and not just cortisol levels, may be an important factor contributing to visceral fat accumulation and associated metabolic complications in humans, and that this effect is mediated in part through increased expression of 11beta-HS-1 in adipose tissue.
cortisol production and clearance are tightly coupled and that the relationship between cortisol production and clearance and visceral obesity and insulin sensitivity is complex.
the hypothalamic-pituatary-adrenal axis may be a potential target for the prevention or treatment of obesity and its metabolic consequences.
